read.sections.1.text.back: A season is a part of the year that has its own kind of weather. Many places far from the equator have four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. These seasons happen because the Earth is tilted as it moves around the Sun. Near the equator, the air is warm all year, so usually what there is is a rainy season and a dry season. In South Asia and Southeast Asia, seasonal winds called monsoons bring heavy rain for several months. In India, for example, most of the year's rain falls between June and September.
read.sections.1.text.source: A season is a part of the year with its own kind of weather. Far from the equator, many places have four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. These seasons happen because Earth is tilted as it travels around the Sun. Near the equator, it is warm all year, so the seasons are usually rainy or dry instead. In South Asia and Southeast Asia, a seasonal wind called the monsoon brings heavy rain for several months. In India, for example, most of the year's rain falls between June and September.

read.sections.0.text.back: Weather is the state of the air at one time and in one place. Weather can be hot, cold, wet, dry or windy, and can change within a few minutes. Climate is the pattern of weather that usually happens in a place over a long time. To describe a climate, scientists usually study weather records for at least 30 years. Look at Sunrise School. This afternoon's heavy rain is weather. For 30 years, the rainy season has always been much wetter than the dry season, and that fact is climate. Here is an easy way to remember the difference: weather is what you experience today, while climate is what you expect.
read.sections.0.text.source: Weather is what the air is like at one time and place. It can be hot, cold, wet, dry or windy, and it can change in minutes. Climate is the usual pattern of weather in a place over a long time. To describe a climate, scientists usually study at least 30 years of weather records. Look at Sunrise School. Heavy rain this afternoon is weather. The fact that the rainy season has been much wetter than the dry season for 30 years is climate. Here is a simple way to remember the difference: weather is what you get today, but climate is what you expect.

read.sections.2.heading.back: People adapt to climate and seasons
read.sections.2.heading.source: People adapt to climate and seasons

read.sections.2.text.back: People change their way of life to fit the climate where they live. This change is called adaptation. In hot, dry places, like parts of Mali and Yemen, many buildings have thick mud-brick walls that help keep rooms cool. In Mongolia, some herders move their animals between summer camps and winter camps. In many farming communities, people start planting when the rainy season arrives. Sunrise School adapts too. Roofed walkways keep students dry, and drinking-water stations help on hot days. Good adaptation is based on evidence and is useful for everyone, including people who use wheelchairs.
read.sections.2.text.source: People change how they live to suit their climate. These changes are called adaptations. In hot, dry places, such as parts of Mali and Yemen, many buildings have thick mud-brick walls that help keep rooms cool. In Mongolia, some herders move their animals between summer and winter camps. In many farming communities, people plant crops when the rainy season begins. Sunrise School adapts too. Covered walkways keep students dry, and water stations help on hot days. A good adaptation is based on evidence and works for everyone, including people who use wheelchairs.

watch.summary.back: This video explains how the Earth's climate is changing. Some gases in the air, like carbon dioxide, trap heat from the Sun. These gases work a little like the glass walls of a greenhouse, which keep plants warm. People burn coal, oil and gas to get energy. This adds more of these gases to the air, so the Earth gets warmer. The video says that a warmer Earth changes weather patterns. Large sheets of ice in Greenland and Antarctica are melting, and sea level is rising. Now some places have stronger storms and heavier rain. Other places have longer dry periods. This can make food crops harder to grow. The video ends with a hopeful idea. People can use power from the sun and wind, which does not add these gases.

They work a bit like the glass walls of a greenhouse, which keep plants warm. People burn coal, oil and gas for energy. This adds more of these gases to the air, so Earth is getting warmer. The video says a warmer Earth changes weather patterns. Large areas of ice in Greenland and Antarctica are melting, and the sea is rising. Some places now get stronger storms and heavier rain. Other places get longer dry times. This can make it harder to grow food. The video ends with a hopeful idea. People can use power from the sun and wind, which does not add these gases.
